title: How teachers can recommend a spelling method to parents
meta_description: A teacher can recommend a spelling method to parents with one short note that names the method, the first practice step and the time, and invites a reply.
keywords: look cover write check note home
hero_image_alt: Three plain pink envelopes, a blank folded note card, a small brass handbell and a wooden peg on a navy painted desk, seen from above.
content_html:
A teacher can recommend a spelling method to parents by sending home one short, specific instruction rather than a general explanation: name the method, say what the first practice session looks like, and say how long it takes. Education Endowment Foundation guidance says general information is not sufficient unless it is linked to specific actions, and asks schools to tailor communications so that the conversation runs both ways.

Key takeaways

  • A note that names the method, describes the first practice session and gives a time is more useful to a parent than a general account of why spelling matters, because the Education Endowment Foundation (EEF) says information needs to be linked to specific actions.
  • The message can travel in a channel the school already uses, such as the reading record or a weekly sheet. The EEF describes short letters and texts as typically low cost and straightforward to introduce.
  • A reply line on the note opens a conversation. The EEF reports that around half of parents say they have not been consulted.
  • A teacher can describe a routine without promising a result, which keeps the note accurate and the parent’s expectations realistic.
  • Teachers who want a ready made sheet can make one for free on the Spelling Nest teachers page, with or without the app.

Why does a general explanation of a spelling method not reach parents?

A general explanation of a spelling method leaves a parent knowing why spelling matters but not what to do at half past six on a Tuesday. That gap is the likely reason a well meant paragraph in a newsletter changes little at home: the parent agrees, then has no first step to take.

The EEF’s guidance report, Working with Parents to Support Children’s Learning, points the same way. Its second recommendation is to provide practical strategies to support learning at home, and it says schools can support parents with practical guidance and encouragement about the sorts of things they can do at home. It adds that general information on child development or curriculum content gives helpful context but is "not sufficient unless it is linked to specific actions". Among the skills it names for early primary are activities that target reading, with spellings listed alongside letter sounds and word reading.

The same report’s third recommendation asks schools to tailor communications to encourage positive dialogue about learning. For a spelling method, that means writing to the parent as a partner in a routine, not as the recipient of a notice.

What should a note about look, cover, write, check say?

A note about look, cover, write, check should say four things: the name of the method, what the child does first, how long it takes, and how the parent can reply. Everything else can be left out of the first note.

The method has four steps. The child looks at the word, covers it, writes it from memory, and then uncovers it and checks it letter by letter. The step that matters most is the covering, because writing from memory is what makes the child retrieve the spelling rather than copy it. The Spelling Nest page on look, cover, write, check sets out each step, and the post on how to do look, cover, write, check properly covers the mistakes families most often make.

Here is one way a note might read. It is written for a parent, and a teacher is free to change every word.

Each week your child brings home a list of spellings. We practise them with look, cover, write, check. About ten minutes is enough. Your child looks at one word, covers it, writes it from memory, then uncovers it and checks every letter. If it is wrong, they write it again on the next line. Please do not say the spelling aloud while they write. If anything is unclear, write a line in the reading record and I will reply.

The note is short on purpose. It carries an action a parent can take tonight, a time limit that makes the task look finite, and one instruction about what not to do. Three details are worth keeping whatever the wording:

  • Name the method once and use the same name every time. A parent who hears "look, cover, write, check" on Monday and "the spelling strategy" on Friday may not connect the two.
  • State the time. A task with an end is easier to start than one without. Ten minutes is a figure a teacher can adjust to the age of the class.
  • Say what the parent should not do. The most common problem with home practice is a well meaning adult supplying the answer, and one plain sentence heads it off better than a paragraph of explanation.

How can a teacher send it home without extra work?

A teacher can send a spelling method home without extra work by attaching it to something that already goes home each week, such as the spelling list or the reading record.

The EEF report describes school communications such as short, termly letters and weekly texts as typically low cost and straightforward to introduce, and says messages are likely to be more effective if they are personalised, linked to learning and framed positively. It also says that where there are important messages for parents who are less involved, a face to face conversation, a phone call or a text message is likely to work better than a generic email or letter home. For a spelling note, that suggests keeping it short, putting it where parents already look, and following it with a word at pick up or parents’ evening where the chance arises.

A teacher who already writes out a weekly list has two efficient options: paste the note once at the top of the list and leave it there all term, or use a printed sheet that carries the method on it, so the instruction travels with the words each week.

The Spelling Nest teachers page offers the second option. According to that page, a teacher can make a weekly spelling sheet, or a whole year of them at once, as a PDF. The sheet is made by the page inside the teacher’s own browser, so the words, the school name and the logo are not sent to Spelling Nest or anyone else, and there is no account to create. Each sheet carries a QR code that a parent scans to load the words into the app at home; the code holds a web link with that sheet’s words, its title and the test date, and no pupil names or school details. The sheets are free for schools and work without the app, and a teacher can use their own spelling scheme, provided its licence allows the lists to be printed.

How should a teacher respond when parents want to help?

A teacher should respond to a parent who wants to help by asking what the parent has already tried, and then giving one adjustment, not a new system.

The report says consulting parents about how they can be involved is likely to be valuable, and that around half of parents say they have not been consulted. A single line on the note, such as "tell me if the ten minutes does not fit your evenings", is a small and cheap way to begin that consultation, because it invites information the teacher would not otherwise get. That is a practical suggestion drawn from the recommendation, not something the report itself prescribes.

Parents who want to help sometimes want to help too much. The EEF report advises caution about encouraging direct parental involvement in homework tasks, especially for older children, while recommending that parents encourage a regular routine and good study habits. For spelling, that means the parent provides the time, the quiet and the covering, and the child writes the word. Sitting with a child is different from supplying the letters.

Where a parent says practice is a struggle at home, the teacher can point to the Spelling Nest page on how spelling sticks, which sets out why short, repeated practice on separate days tends to work better than one long session.

What should a teacher leave out of the note?

A teacher should leave out any promise about results, any comparison between children, and any long explanation of why the method works. Each makes a note longer without making it easier to act on.

The EEF is open that the evidence in this area is not yet as strong as it would like, so a note promising better test scores claims more than the research supports. A note that describes a routine claims only what the teacher can stand behind. A note that mentions how other children are getting on turns a routine into a ranking, so that goes too. Parents told what the school does and how long it takes can judge for themselves whether it is working.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best length for a note to parents about spelling?

About five or six short sentences: the method, the first action, the time, the instruction about what not to do, and a line inviting a reply. A longer account can be offered separately to parents who want it.

Should a teacher explain the research behind look, cover, write, check?

Not in the first note. The EEF report says general information is not sufficient unless it is linked to specific actions, so the first note should say what to do. An explanation can follow at a parents’ evening or on a separate page for those who ask.

Does telling parents about a method improve spelling test results?

The sources read for this post do not show that. The EEF says the evidence in this area is not yet as strong as it would like, so a teacher is better placed describing a routine than promising a result.

Can a teacher use their own spelling scheme with the Spelling Nest sheets?

Yes, according to the Spelling Nest teachers page. The sheets use whatever words a teacher types or pastes, and if the lists come from a published scheme, the teacher should check that their licence allows the lists to be printed. The sheet is made inside the teacher’s own browser, and nothing typed into it is sent to Spelling Nest.

For a sheet that carries the method home with the words, see the Spelling Nest teachers page.
